specs.q: How is a coroutine different from a thread?
specs.angle: A coroutine is a heap object scheduled onto a thread pool, not an OS thread: a few hundred bytes versus a ~512KB-1MB thread stack, so 100k coroutines are routine and 100k threads OOM. Must land the corollary a weak candidate misses: coroutines do not make blocking code non-blocking — a coroutine calling a blocking API occupies its carrier thread exactly like any other code.

specs.q: Does marking a function `suspend` make it run off the main thread?
specs.angle: No. `suspend` is a compiler contract (it adds a Continuation parameter), not a threading keyword; the function runs on whatever dispatcher the caller was on. Main-safety is the callee's responsibility via an internal `withContext(ioDispatcher)`, so `suspend fun` + Room/Retrofit is safe only because those libraries dispatch internally.

specs.q: What is the difference between `delay(1000)` and `Thread.sleep(1000)` inside a coroutine?
specs.angle: `delay` suspends: it schedules a resume on the dispatcher's timer and hands the thread back. `Thread.sleep` parks the OS thread, so four sleeping coroutines on a 4-core `Dispatchers.Default` wedge the entire pool. Add the test angle: `delay` is skipped by `runTest`'s virtual clock, `Thread.sleep` genuinely sleeps and makes the suite slow and flaky.

specs.q: What does a single suspension point actually cost at runtime?
specs.angle: The fast path is nearly free: if the callee returns without suspending it returns the value directly instead of `COROUTINE_SUSPENDED`, and one state-machine object is reused for the whole call chain — single-digit nanoseconds. The cost shows up when it really suspends: spilling every live local into a field, the `switch (label)` re-entry, and possibly a dispatch (a Handler post or a scheduler task, ~microseconds) — which is precisely why `withContext` inside a hot loop is a measurable regression.

specs.q: Turn a callback-based API into a suspend function.
specs.angle: `suspendCancellableCoroutine` plus `invokeOnCancellation { call.cancel() }`; the continuation must be resumed exactly once (a second `resume` throws IllegalStateException). Explain why `suspendCoroutine` is the wrong tool: it has no cancellation hook, so a cancelled coroutine leaves the callback registered and the caller waits forever. Show the resource-carrying case with the `resume(value) { ... }` onCancellation overload.

specs.q: A callback resumes your continuation from a random OkHttp thread. How does the coroutine get back onto the main thread?
specs.angle: `ContinuationInterceptor` is a context element: the dispatcher wraps your continuation in a `DispatchedContinuation`, and `resumeWith` consults `isDispatchNeeded`/`dispatch` to re-post onto the target. That is exactly why `Dispatchers.Main.immediate` returns false from `isDispatchNeeded` when already on Main and skips a Handler round trip, and why `Unconfined` never re-posts. Tie it to `CoroutineStart.DEFAULT` vs `UNDISPATCHED` vs `ATOMIC` and the ordering surprise that a `launch` body has not started yet when the next line executes.

specs.q: Why can't you call a suspend function directly from `onCreate()` or a click listener, and what do you do instead?
specs.angle: A suspend function needs a Continuation, so it can only be called from inside a coroutine — you need a `CoroutineScope`, and Android hands you `viewModelScope` / `lifecycleScope`. Explicitly reject the two wrong fixes a junior offers: wrapping it in `runBlocking`, and making the framework callback itself suspend. The point of the scope is that it binds the work's lifetime to the component's.

specs.q: What is a `CoroutineContext`, and what does the `+` operator actually do?
specs.angle: It is an immutable, type-indexed set — a map from `Key` to `Element` — and the four elements you meet are `Job`, `ContinuationInterceptor` (the dispatcher), `CoroutineName` and `CoroutineExceptionHandler`. `a + b` is right-biased: the right operand replaces any same-key element. Show `coroutineContext[Job]`, `minusKey`, and the inheritance rule — a child copies the parent's context but substitutes its own new Job.

specs.q: What does `CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Main + SupervisorJob())` create, and what happens to it after you call `cancel()`?
specs.angle: A CoroutineScope is nothing but a holder for a CoroutineContext; the `CoroutineScope(...)` factory adds a Job if you did not supply one, and you own cancelling it. The trap that gets people: a cancelled scope is dead permanently — `launch` on it returns an already-cancelled Job and the block never runs, with no exception and no log. If you want to reuse the scope, use `coroutineContext.cancelChildren()` instead.

specs.q: `Job` vs `SupervisorJob` — and why does `launch(SupervisorJob())` supervise nothing?
specs.angle: SupervisorJob only changes how failures of *its own children* propagate. Passing one into `launch` makes it that coroutine's own Job, so the siblings you wanted isolated are unaffected — and the new Job is still parented to the enclosing job, so a failure propagates upward anyway. The only correct forms are `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + ...)` and `supervisorScope { }`.

specs.q: Why is `GlobalScope` effectively banned, and what replaces it?
specs.angle: No parent, no Job you can cancel, and uncaught exceptions go straight to the thread's default handler and crash the app — the coroutine outlives the screen while holding whatever it captured. Replacements: an injected application-scoped `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default)` for fire-and-forget, or WorkManager when the work must survive process death. Mention the `@DelicateCoroutinesApi` opt-in as the library telling you the same thing.

specs.q: The user taps Save and immediately backs out. `viewModelScope` is cancelled and the POST dies. Fix it, and defend the design.
specs.angle: This is structured concurrency working as specified — no work outlives its scope — so the fix is to give the work a scope whose lifetime matches the *work*: an `@ApplicationScope` singleton scope owned by the repository, or WorkManager with unique work for anything that must survive process death. Argue both sides (a leaked app-scoped write vs a lost user edit) and name the three wrong answers: `NonCancellable`, `GlobalScope`, and launching in the ViewModel and hoping.

specs.q: Where exactly does a `CoroutineExceptionHandler` fire, and where does it silently do nothing?
specs.angle: It is consulted only by the *root* coroutine of a scope. Installing it on a child `launch` is ignored — the exception goes to the parent — and it never applies to `async`, whose exception sits in the Deferred until `await()`. Direct children of `supervisorScope` behave as roots, so a handler there does fire. With no handler the exception reaches `Thread.uncaughtExceptionHandler` and crashes the Android process.

specs.q: Fetch profile, settings and feed in parallel. Show the code, then explain exactly what happens when one of them fails.
specs.angle: `coroutineScope { val a = async{}; val b = async{}; awaitAll(a, b) }` is fail-fast: the failing child cancels its siblings and `coroutineScope` rethrows at the first `await`. Contrast the partial-results variant (`supervisorScope` + per-branch `runCatching`, remembering that an `async` under a supervisor holds its exception until awaited and loses it entirely if never awaited), and name the `async(start = LAZY)` trap where a Deferred that is never awaited makes `coroutineScope` hang forever on a child that never started.

specs.q: Race a cache read against a network call and take whichever answers first. What are the options, and what leaks?
specs.angle: `select { cacheDeferred.onAwait { }; networkDeferred.onAwait { } }` returns the first branch — but the losing coroutine keeps running unless you cancel it, so you leak a request and possibly a registered callback; wrapping in `coroutineScope` and cancelling the loser explicitly is the fix. Cover `onTimeout`/`onReceive`, the experimental status of parts of `select`, and the simpler alternatives that usually win a code review: `withTimeoutOrNull`, `merge(a, b).first()`.

specs.q: Cancellation is cooperative. What does that mean, and how do you make a CPU-bound loop cancellable?
specs.angle: `cancel()` only moves the Job to Cancelling and arms the *next suspension point* to throw — a `while (true) { crunch() }` with no suspension runs to completion regardless. Add `ensureActive()` (throws) or check `isActive` (returns cleanly), and use `yield()` when you also want to let other coroutines on that dispatcher run. Second half: `cancel()` returns immediately, so use `cancelAndJoin()` when you need the coroutine to actually be finished — the classic source of flaky tests.

specs.q: Why does `try { api.load() } catch (e: Exception) { showError() }` break cancellation?
specs.angle: Cancellation is delivered as a `CancellationException` thrown from the suspension point, so a catch-all swallows the signal: the coroutine 'recovers' and keeps executing while its Job is already Cancelling, and the user sees an error toast on a screen they already left. The rules to state: rethrow `CancellationException` (or catch only the specific exception), call `currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()` at the top of the catch, and never wrap a suspend call in `runCatching`, which catches Throwable.

specs.q: How do you release a resource in a `finally` block when the coroutine has already been cancelled?
specs.angle: In a cancelled coroutine every suspension point throws immediately, so a `finally` that suspends — closing a session, flushing analytics — never completes. Wrap only that cleanup in `withContext(NonCancellable)`. Insist on the boundary: a few lines with a bounded runtime, never a wrapper around the real work, because `NonCancellable` makes the block genuinely uninterruptible. Mention `job.invokeOnCompletion` and `Closeable.use` for the non-suspending case.

specs.q: `withTimeout` vs `withTimeoutOrNull` — and what do people get wrong about both?
specs.angle: withTimeout throws `TimeoutCancellationException`, withTimeoutOrNull returns null. Trap one: that exception *is* a `CancellationException`, so an outer catch-all swallows it and an enclosing coroutine can be fooled into thinking it was cancelled. Trap two: the timeout can only fire at a suspension point, so it will not interrupt `Thread.sleep` or a blocking JNI call — and a result produced right at the deadline is discarded, which is a resource leak if it owned a stream.

specs.q: A `suspendCancellableCoroutine` wrapping a download is cancelled at the exact instant the response arrives. Who closes the response body?
specs.angle: Nobody — the resume/cancel race means the value passed to `resume()` is dropped on the floor when the continuation is already cancelled, leaking the `Response`, `Cursor` or file descriptor. Fixes: the `resume(value) { ... }` onCancellation overload, `Channel(onUndeliveredElement = { it.close() })` for the channel case, and `CoroutineStart.ATOMIC` when the launch itself must not be skipped. Explain why a hand-rolled try/finally across a suspension point does not close this window.

specs.q: Compare `launch`, `async`, `withContext`, `coroutineScope`, `runBlocking` and `produce`: what each returns, which ones suspend, and how each surfaces an exception.
specs.angle: A table the candidate should be able to reconstruct from first principles: launch → Job, fire-and-forget, exception straight to the parent; async → Deferred, exception parked until `await()`; withContext/coroutineScope → suspending, return a value, rethrow to the caller; runBlocking → blocks a thread and is not a suspend function; produce → hot ReceiveChannel. Include the four `CoroutineStart` modes and the rule that a single call should use `withContext`, never `async { }.await()`.

specs.q: Why is `runBlocking` banned in production Android code, and where is it legitimately correct?
specs.angle: It blocks the calling thread and runs an event loop on it until the block finishes — on Main that is a guaranteed ANR. The killer detail: `runBlocking { withContext(Dispatchers.Main) { } }` called *from* the main thread deadlocks, because the looper is blocked and can never dispatch the inner block. Legitimate uses: `fun main()`, JUnit tests, and framework entry points that must return synchronously (ContentProvider, a legacy Worker). Everywhere else it means the caller should have been suspend.

specs.q: What does `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` actually do, and what does it cost?
specs.angle: It suspends, creates a child coroutine with the merged context, dispatches to the target, runs the block, then dispatches back and returns the value — up to two thread hand-offs per call, so calling it per item inside a loop instead of hoisting it around the loop is a real regression. Three semantics to nail: it is strictly sequential (never a concurrency tool), it is cancelled with its caller, and a `Job` you pass in is replaced by the new coroutine's own Job — `withContext(IO + Job())` detaches nothing.

specs.q: You need at most 4 concurrent uploads. `Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4)`, a `Semaphore(4)`, or `flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4)`?
specs.angle: limitedParallelism is a *view* over the shared CoroutineScheduler that caps how many tasks are dispatched simultaneously — a coroutine that suspends (exactly what an upload does while awaiting IO) gives the slot back, so it does not bound logical concurrency at all; `Semaphore(4)` or `flatMapMerge(4)` do. Use the answer to explain the shared IO/Default pool, IO's elastic 64-thread limit (`kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism`) layered on CPU permits, why a blocking call on Default starves it, and when `Executor.asCoroutineDispatcher()` — which you must close — is still justified.

specs.q: `Mutex` vs `synchronized` in suspending code.
specs.angle: `synchronized` takes a JVM monitor bound to a *thread*; the compiler refuses a suspension point inside it, and if it did not, a coroutine could suspend while still owning a monitor that another coroutine on the same thread needs. `Mutex.withLock` is suspending, cancellation-aware and FIFO-fair — but explicitly **not reentrant**, so a nested `withLock` on the same mutex deadlocks permanently — and it is far slower than an atomic under contention.

specs.q: Three coroutines increment a shared counter and you get the wrong number. Rank the fixes.
specs.angle: Preference order: don't share (confine the state to one coroutine or a `limitedParallelism(1)` dispatcher), then immutable state behind `MutableStateFlow.update { it.copy(...) }`, then `AtomicInteger`/`AtomicReference`, and only then `Mutex`. Two traps must appear: `update {}` is a compare-and-set loop so the lambda **can run more than once** and must be side-effect-free, and `state.value = state.value + 1` is a lost-update race — which is the entire reason `update` exists.

specs.q: What is a Flow, and what happens the moment you call `collect`?
specs.angle: A Flow is essentially a suspend function that can return many values: `collect` runs the builder block in the *collector's own coroutine*, and each `emit` is a direct suspending call into the collector's lambda, so intermediate operators are just wrappers around the collector. Nothing runs until a terminal operator is invoked, and every new collector re-runs the whole chain. Contrast intermediate (returns a Flow, lazy, free) vs terminal (suspends, does the work).

specs.q: Tour the Flow operators you use daily, and name the two that people misuse.
specs.angle: map/filter, `transform` (0..n emissions per input — the escape hatch when map is not enough), onEach, onStart for a Loading state, scan/runningFold for accumulation; terminals first/single/toList/fold plus `launchIn(scope)` as sugar for `scope.launch { collect() }`. The two misused: `onCompletion`, which receives the cause including a CancellationException, runs on failure, but cannot swallow the exception; and `first()`, which cancels the upstream after one value — correct for a one-shot read, silently wrong when you meant to observe.

specs.q: `flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(x) } }` crashes at runtime. Why, and what is the rule?
specs.angle: 'Flow invariant is violated: emission from another coroutine context' — `emit` must be called from the same coroutine that called `collect`, otherwise the collector's context and Job no longer govern the emission and cancellation breaks. The correct tools are `flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)`, which changes the context of everything *upstream of that operator only* by inserting an extra coroutine and channel, and `channelFlow` when you genuinely need concurrent emitters. Note that a second `flowOn` lower in the chain does not undo the first.

specs.q: Exception transparency: what can `catch` catch, and what escapes it?
specs.angle: `catch` sees only exceptions thrown *upstream of itself* — a crash inside the `collect { }` lambda flies straight past it, which is why you move that body into an `onEach { }` above the `catch` if you want it covered. Also: wrapping your own `emit` in try/catch violates transparency because it can capture the *downstream's* exception; `catch` may emit a fallback value; and `retry`/`retryWhen` are built on exactly this machinery.

specs.q: Explain `buffer`, `conflate` and `collectLatest` at the channel level, and what operator fusion does to them.
specs.angle: `buffer(capacity, onBufferOverflow)` inserts a Channel plus a second coroutine so producer and collector run concurrently; `conflate()` is exactly `buffer(CONFLATED)`; `collectLatest` buffers nothing at all — it cancels and restarts the *collector body* on each new value, so the producer still runs flat out and a slow body may never complete once. Then the part almost nobody knows: adjacent `flowOn`/`buffer`/`conflate` operators are **fused** into a single channel with combined capacity, so `.conflate().buffer(10)` is not two buffers.

specs.q: Build search-as-you-type and defend the position of every operator.
specs.angle: `query.debounce(300).filter { it.length >= 2 }.distinctUntilChanged().flatMapLatest { repo.search(it) }.catch { emit(Empty) }` — debounce before the network call, distinctUntilChanged to kill the delete-then-retype duplicate, flatMapLatest so the in-flight request is cancelled. Traps to name: debounce also delays the *first* keystroke, a user typing continuously never triggers debounce at all (use `sample` when you need periodic updates), `distinctUntilChanged` compares with `equals` so a wrapper data class can defeat it, and `debounce`/`sample` still need `@OptIn(FlowPreview::class)`.

specs.q: `combine` vs `zip` vs `merge` — which one builds a UiState from three sources?
specs.angle: `combine` re-emits on *any* source change but only starts once **every** source has emitted at least once — one cold flow that never emits means your screen never renders, which is why StateFlows combine safely and a filtered Room flow may not. `zip` is lock-step pairing and completes with the shortest source; `merge` interleaves same-typed flows with no correlation. Warn about the combine re-emission storm driving recomposition, and prefer one `UiState` flow over five stacked combines.

specs.q: Add retry with exponential backoff to a network Flow.
specs.angle: `retryWhen { cause, attempt -> if (cause is IOException && attempt < 3) { delay(1000L * (1 shl attempt.toInt()) + Random.nextLong(500)); true } else false }` — the jitter matters because synchronised clients thundering-herd the backend on recovery. Mechanics to land: `retry` re-collects the **entire upstream** (fine for a cold flow, meaningless for a hot one), the attempt counter is zero-based, you must not retry 4xx, and stacking this on top of OkHttp and WorkManager retry gives you three compounding backoffs.

specs.q: `flow { }` vs `channelFlow { }` vs `callbackFlow { }` — how do you choose?
specs.angle: `flow {}` is the default: cold, sequential, context-preserving and cheapest (no channel allocated). `channelFlow {}` exists precisely to break the emission-context rule — `send` is thread-safe so multiple child coroutines can emit concurrently — at the cost of a Channel plus an extra coroutine. `callbackFlow` is `channelFlow` specialised for register/unregister of a listener, and its non-negotiable contract is `awaitClose`.

specs.q: Wrap a listener-based API (say `LocationManager`) in a Flow. What goes wrong?
specs.angle: Omitting `awaitClose` throws at runtime — it is both the suspension that keeps the flow alive and the only place you unregister, so forgetting it leaks the listener. Then: you cannot `send` from a non-suspending callback, so it is `trySend`, whose default RENDEZVOUS capacity makes it **fail silently** unless you pass a capacity or add `.buffer()`/`.conflate()`. Check `trySend().isSuccess`, or you will quietly drop location fixes and never know.

specs.q: Enumerate the Channel capacities and `BufferOverflow` modes, then design a telemetry pipeline that must never block the producer.
specs.angle: RENDEZVOUS (0), BUFFERED (64 by default via `kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer`), CONFLATED, UNLIMITED, plus SUSPEND / DROP_OLDEST / DROP_LATEST — the right answer is a bounded buffer with DROP_OLDEST, never UNLIMITED, which is an OOM with extra steps. Also cover `close()` (receivers drain, then finish) vs `cancel()` (buffer discarded), ClosedSendChannelException, `onUndeliveredElement` for elements that own resources, and that a Channel is hot and single-delivery — two receivers split the values, they do not each get all of them.

specs.q: One-shot events (navigate, show a snackbar): `Channel`, `SharedFlow`, or state? Argue all three.
specs.angle: `SharedFlow(replay = 0)` drops events emitted while the UI is STOPPED — exactly the window `repeatOnLifecycle` creates — so a navigation event vanishes on rotation. A `Channel` gives exactly-once delivery to a single consumer but breaks with two collectors and still loses everything on process death. Modelling the event as state with an explicit `onEventConsumed()` survives both, at the cost of boilerplate. The candidate must take a position and name which failure mode they are knowingly accepting.

specs.q: StateFlow vs SharedFlow vs LiveData — which do you expose for UI state, and why is LiveData out?
specs.angle: StateFlow: always has a value, conflated, deduped by `equals`, `.value` readable synchronously — the default for UI state. SharedFlow: no initial value, configurable replay, no dedup — for events and broadcast. LiveData: lifecycle-aware but main-thread-bound, no operators, no KMP, and superseded by `collectAsStateWithLifecycle`/`repeatOnLifecycle`. Land the key asymmetry: StateFlow is *not* lifecycle-aware on its own, which is the entire reason the lifecycle-aware collectors exist.

specs.q: You update the state in the ViewModel but the UI does not change. Why?
specs.angle: StateFlow conflates by `equals`, so re-emitting an equal value emits nothing: mutating a `MutableList` in place and assigning the same reference back, or a data class with an `Array` field whose `equals` is identity-based, produce a silent no-op. Fix with immutable state and `update { it.copy(...) }`. Then the other half of conflation: intermediate values from a fast producer are dropped *by design*, so a StateFlow is the wrong type for a stream of events you must not miss.

specs.q: Tune `MutableSharedFlow(replay, extraBufferCapacity, onBufferOverflow)` for an in-app event bus.
specs.angle: With replay = 0 and extraBufferCapacity = 0 the buffer is zero, so `emit` **suspends until every subscriber has collected the value** — one slow collector stalls your ViewModel — and `tryEmit` always returns false. The usual configuration is `extraBufferCapacity = 1` with `onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST`, which makes emit never suspend. Add `subscriptionCount` for starting/stopping upstream work, and the warning that replay > 0 re-delivers to every new subscriber, which is wrong for navigation events.

specs.q: `stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), Loading)` — justify every argument.
specs.angle: WhileSubscribed starts the upstream on the first subscriber and stops it `stopTimeoutMillis` after the last one leaves; 5000 is a grace window sized to cover an Activity recreation, so a rotation does not tear down and rebuild a Room query or a socket — it has nothing to do with process death. Also: `replayExpirationMillis` defaults to `Long.MAX_VALUE`, so the cached value survives the stop (pass 0 to force a refresh); Eagerly and Lazily never stop the upstream; and the suspending `stateIn(scope)` overload waits for the first value, so it can hang forever on a source that never emits.

specs.q: What exactly are `viewModelScope` and `lifecycleScope`, and when is each cancelled?
specs.angle: Both are plain CoroutineScopes stored on their owner: `viewModelScope` = `SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate`, cancelled in `onCleared()`; `lifecycleScope` = the same context, cancelled at `onDestroy`. Traps: in a Fragment use `viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope`, because the Fragment outlives its view on the back stack; and `Main.immediate` means the block can start synchronously, which is why a unit test that forgets `Dispatchers.setMain` sees different ordering.

specs.q: Why was `lifecycleScope.launchWhenStarted { }` deprecated?
specs.angle: It suspends the *consumer* at STOP but leaves the upstream producer alive and hot — the Room cursor, the location callback, the socket stay registered and keep producing into a buffer nobody reads, and the suspended collector still holds its captured view. `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)` instead *cancels* the entire collection and restarts it on the next START. `flowWithLifecycle` is the operator form (implemented over callbackFlow + repeatOnLifecycle) — fine for one flow, but it allocates per flow, so nest multiple collects inside a single `repeatOnLifecycle` block.

specs.q: `collectAsState()` vs `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` in Compose — and what does neither of them fix?
specs.angle: `collectAsState` keeps collecting while the app is backgrounded, because composition is not lifecycle-aware; `collectAsStateWithLifecycle` wraps collection in `repeatOnLifecycle(minActiveState = STARTED)`, and that parameter is configurable (RESUMED for a camera preview). Traps: a flow constructed inline in the composable is a brand-new instance on every recomposition (hoist it or `remember` it), a non-StateFlow requires an explicit `initialValue`, and neither operator reduces the recomposition cost of a state object whose identity changes on every emission.

specs.q: The user takes a phone call, Android kills the process, they come back. What happened to your StateFlow?
specs.angle: It is gone — StateFlow, SharedFlow and all in-memory ViewModel state are process-scoped. Only `SavedStateHandle` survives, and `savedStateHandle.getStateFlow(key, default)` is its flow-shaped API. Cover what belongs there (ids, query text, scroll key — small, parcelable, well under the ~1MB Binder limit before TransactionTooLargeException) versus what should simply be re-read from Room or the network, and explicitly kill the widespread confusion that `WhileSubscribed(5000)` or `viewModelScope` has anything to do with process death.

specs.q: Your coroutine test hangs, or fails with 'After waiting for 60s, the test coroutine is not completing'. Debug it.
specs.angle: `runTest` waits for every coroutine in the TestScope to finish, so a collector on a hot flow (`stateIn`, a MutableSharedFlow) never completes — launch it in `backgroundScope`, or use Turbine, which cancels its own collector. Other causes to enumerate: `StandardTestDispatcher` queues everything until you call `advanceUntilIdle()`/`runCurrent()`, so a 'nothing happened' assertion is usually a missing advance; `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` hides genuine ordering bugs; every TestDispatcher in a test must share the same `testScheduler` or virtual time diverges; and testing `WhileSubscribed(5_000)` needs a real subscriber plus `advanceTimeBy(5_001)`.
